newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks verify 11 claims for dormant wealth.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks verify 11 claims for dormant wealth.

text.p: A Swiss banking ombudsman in charge of seeking out dormant accounts of Holocaust victims said on Tuesday that banks had confirmed 11 valid requests for 1.6 million Swiss francs ($1.3 million) in unclaimed wealth.

Three of the 11 legitimate claims -- a small fraction of the nearly 900 detailed inquiries already submitted -- were held in the name of bank customers murdered by the Nazis, Ombudsman Hanspeter Haeni said in a statement prepared for delivery at a news conference.
"Two other customers were Jews who lived in Romania and were totally dispossessed during the war on account of discriminatory legislation," Haeni added.
He did not name the customers or the banks involved.

Haeni, whose work has been dismissed by Jewish critics as a "cruel hoax" designed simply to protect Swiss banks, said his office would continue to act as the central contact point for Holocaust account inquiries for an indefinite period.

He said up to 20 detailed inquiries in the form of questionnaires were coming in every day almost a year after his search began, and that he would make another public appearance in mid-1997 to give an update on the status of the hunt.
Swiss banks deny accusations by Jewish groups and plaintiffs in two class-action suits that they may be sitting on billions of dollars in unclaimed wealth left behind by Hitler's victims.

The Swiss Bankers Association industry group said in February that 38.7 million Swiss francs ($30.7 million) in dormant World War Two-era accounts was still lodged in Swiss banks that had lost contact with the original owners.
Not all of this money necessarily belonged to Holocaust victims, Swiss bankers pointed out.

To probe charges of a cover-up, major Jewish groups and Swiss banks agreed in May to set up an independent panel headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul Volcker to search for any wealth that escaped two previous sweeps by banks.

The commission will also cooperate with a historical panel due to be approved by parliament next month with a broader brief to lay open the scope of Swiss financial dealings with both Nazi Germany and its victims.

Both the Volcker commission and the historians panel will be empowered to lift banking secrecy to probe dormant wartime-era accounts, although these powers will not compromise the confidentiality of accounts held by modern customers.
